subject: ela
intro: Each item gives you a longer literary passage. Read closely, then evaluate the evidence: choose the strongest quotation for an inference, separate what is stated from what is inferred, and explain how a detail proves a claim. Quote exact words from the passage.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The rope bridge swung over the gorge, and Priya counted the slats out loud as she crossed. One. Two. Three. Halfway across, a board cracked under her shoe and dropped into the white water below. She did not look down. She fixed her eyes on the far cliff, loosened her grip on the frayed handrail, and kept counting. Four. Five. Her brother waited on the other side, shouting that she should turn back. Priya answered only with the next number. When her feet finally touched solid rock, her hands were shaking, but she was smiling.

Which quotation gives the strongest evidence that Priya is determined to finish even though she is afraid? Quote the exact words and explain why it is stronger than the other details.
items.answer: The strongest evidence is 'her hands were shaking, but she was smiling.' This single detail shows both her fear (shaking hands) and her resolve to finish anyway (smiling at the end), which directly proves she is determined despite being afraid.

steps: The claim is that Priya is both afraid and determined to finish.
Several details show determination alone, such as 'kept counting' and 'fixed her eyes on the far cliff,' but they do not show fear.
'her hands were shaking, but she was smiling' combines both: shaking hands reveal fear, while the smile after finishing reveals her satisfaction in pushing through.
Because it captures the fear and the determination in one line, it is the strongest evidence for the full claim, stronger than a detail that shows only one half.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The lighthouse had stood dark for three winters. Old Cormac climbed the spiral stairs every evening anyway, lantern in hand, and set a single candle in the cracked glass at the top. Sailors no longer trusted the weak light, and the harbor master had told him to stop wasting his oil. Still, each night the small flame appeared, a stubborn yellow dot against the black coast. Cormac said nothing to anyone. He simply climbed, lit the candle, and sat beside it until dawn, watching the water as if he were waiting for a ship that had been promised long ago.

Which statement is an inference drawn from the passage, not something the text states directly? Identify it and name the detail that the inference is based on.
items.answer: The inference is that Cormac is waiting for someone he lost or expects to return, such as a particular ship or person. The text never states this directly; it is inferred from the detail 'watching the water as if he were waiting for a ship that had been promised long ago.'

steps: The text directly states facts such as the lighthouse being dark for three winters and Cormac lighting a candle each night.
It does not directly state why he keeps lighting the candle.
The phrase 'as if he were waiting for a ship that had been promised long ago' invites the reader to infer he is waiting for someone or something specific.
Because the passage only describes his actions and a comparison, the conclusion that he is waiting for a lost ship or person is an inference, not an explicit statement.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The new coach lined the team up along the baseline. 'Anyone who thinks talent is enough can leave now,' she said. Nobody moved. For the next hour she ran them through the same defensive slide, over and over, until their shirts were soaked and their legs burned. When Devon stumbled and the others groaned, she did not yell. She walked over, showed him the footwork once more, slowly, then said, 'Again.' By the end of practice the slide looked sharp. The coach gathered them at center court. 'That,' she said, 'is what work looks like. Remember the feeling.'

Claim: The coach values effort and improvement more than natural ability. Quote one detail from the passage and explain how it supports this claim.
items.answer: A supporting detail is 'Anyone who thinks talent is enough can leave now.' This shows the coach openly rejects the idea that natural ability alone is what matters, which supports the claim that she values effort over talent. (The detail 'That is what work looks like' or her patiently re-teaching Devon would also work.)

steps: The claim is that the coach values effort and improvement over natural talent.
The line 'Anyone who thinks talent is enough can leave now' directly challenges the value of talent by itself.
By telling players that talent is not enough and then drilling them until the skill improves, the coach connects success to hard work.
This detail therefore supports the claim because it shows her openly ranking effort above raw ability.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Grandmother's kitchen smelled of cardamom and smoke. She never measured anything. A pinch of this, a handful of that, a slow turn of the wooden spoon while she hummed a song with no words. When I asked for the recipe so I could make it at home, she laughed and tapped the side of her head. 'It is not written down,' she said. 'It lives here, and one day it will live in you.' She guided my hands over the pot, letting me feel when the onions were ready by their color and their hiss. I burned the first batch. She only shrugged and started again, patient as the kettle.

Which quotation best supports the inference that the grandmother passes on cooking as a living tradition rather than a fixed set of rules? Quote it and explain your choice.
items.answer: The best quotation is 'It is not written down. It lives here, and one day it will live in you.' This directly contrasts written rules with a tradition carried in a person and handed down, which supports the inference that she treats cooking as a living tradition.

steps: The inference is that cooking is passed on as a living, person-to-person tradition, not as fixed written rules.
Other true details, like 'She never measured anything,' show her informal style but not the idea of passing it on.
'It is not written down. It lives here, and one day it will live in you' explicitly rejects written rules and frames the knowledge as something living that moves to the next person.
Because it captures both halves of the inference, the rejection of fixed rules and the passing on of a living tradition, it is the strongest evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The science fair had ended an hour ago. Most students had packed up their poster boards and gone home, but Mara still stood at her table, frowning at the ribbon she had not won. A judge passing by stopped. 'Your bridge held the most weight of anyone here,' he said. 'Why so glum?' Mara pointed at the winning project, a glittering volcano that erupted on cue. 'People liked the show better,' she said quietly. The judge studied her sturdy little bridge, then her face. 'The flashiest thing in the room is not always the strongest,' he said. 'You will understand that better than most someday.'

One reader claims: 'The passage states directly that Mara's bridge was the best project at the fair.' Is this an explicit statement or an inference? Quote the relevant text and explain.
items.answer: It is an inference, not an explicit statement. The text states directly only that 'Your bridge held the most weight of anyone here.' It never says her bridge was the best project overall, so concluding it was the best is an inference the reader draws, especially since a different project actually won.

steps: Locate what the text actually states: the judge says 'Your bridge held the most weight of anyone here.'
Holding the most weight is one specific measure, not a statement that the bridge was the best overall project.
In fact the glittering volcano won the ribbon, so the text does not claim Mara's was best.
Therefore 'her bridge was the best project' is an inference a reader might draw, not something the passage states directly.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The storm had knocked out the power, and the apartment was dark except for one flashlight. Ten-year-old Theo's little sister whimpered under the blanket every time thunder cracked. Theo did not feel brave. His own heart was pounding, and the wind sounded like something trying to get in. But he made his voice steady and turned the flashlight into a puppet show against the wall, a galloping horse, a flapping bird, a long-eared rabbit. His sister's whimpers turned to giggles. He kept his hands moving even when the thunder made him flinch, because as long as she was laughing she was not afraid.

Which quotation is the strongest evidence that Theo acts brave for his sister's sake even though he is frightened himself? Quote it and explain why it beats the other options.
items.answer: The strongest quotation is 'He kept his hands moving even when the thunder made him flinch, because as long as she was laughing she was not afraid.' It shows his own fear (he flinches), his continued effort (he keeps his hands moving), and his motive (to keep his sister from being afraid), proving he acts brave for her sake.

steps: The claim has three parts: Theo is frightened, he still acts, and he does it for his sister.
'Theo did not feel brave' shows fear but not the reason for acting; the puppet show line shows action but not clearly his fear.
'He kept his hands moving even when the thunder made him flinch, because as long as she was laughing she was not afraid' contains all three parts at once.
Because it ties his fear, his action, and his caring motive together, it is the strongest single piece of evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The market square buzzed at dawn. Vendors stacked oranges into bright pyramids, a baker slid trays of bread into a roaring oven, and somewhere a fiddler tuned a string. But in the doorway of the shuttered bookshop sat a thin gray cat, perfectly still, watching it all with half-closed eyes. While the city rushed and shouted around it, the cat did not move for a long time. Then, as if it had decided the morning was finally worth the trouble, it rose, stretched each leg in turn, and padded slowly into the warm light, unhurried by anyone's noise.

A student wants to prove the claim 'the cat is calm and unbothered by the busy crowd.' Two quotations are offered: A) 'The market square buzzed at dawn.' B) 'unhurried by anyone's noise.' Which is the stronger evidence, and why is the other one weak?
items.answer: Quotation B, 'unhurried by anyone's noise,' is the stronger evidence because it directly describes the cat staying calm despite the surrounding commotion. Quotation A, 'The market square buzzed at dawn,' is weak because it describes the busy setting, not the cat, so it does not support a claim about the cat's calm nature.

steps: The claim is about the cat being calm and unbothered by the crowd.
Quotation A describes the busy market, which is the setting, and says nothing about the cat's reaction.
Quotation B, 'unhurried by anyone's noise,' directly states that the cat is not rushed by the surrounding sounds.
Because B is about the cat and matches the claim, it is the strong evidence; A is a true detail that is off the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Winter clamped down on the village early that year. The river wore a skin of ice, and the trees stood like black iron against the sky. Inside the inn, though, the fire never went out. Travelers stamped the snow from their boots and found bowls of hot stew pressed into their hands before they had even asked. The innkeeper, a round woman with flour on her sleeves, refused payment from those who clearly had none. 'The road is cruel enough,' she would say, ladling out another helping. 'A person should be able to count on a warm room somewhere.' By spring, half the county knew her name.

The author uses figurative language in 'The river wore a skin of ice, and the trees stood like black iron against the sky.' A reader claims this proves the weather is cruel like the innkeeper. Explain why this reading misuses the evidence, and state what the figurative language actually shows.
items.answer: The reading misuses the evidence because it takes the figurative description of harsh winter and wrongly attaches it to the innkeeper, who is shown as warm and generous, the opposite of cruel. The figurative language 'a skin of ice' and 'trees stood like black iron' actually shows how cold and harsh the outside weather is, which contrasts with the warmth inside the inn rather than describing the innkeeper.

steps: Identify what the figurative language describes: the river and trees in harsh winter, showing a cold, severe outdoor setting.
The claim links this cruelty to the innkeeper, but the innkeeper gives free stew and a warm room, so she is kind, not cruel.
The cold imagery is set against 'the fire never went out' inside, creating a contrast between the cruel outdoors and the warm inn.
So the evidence shows a harsh setting that highlights the innkeeper's warmth by contrast; using it to call her cruel misreads the figurative language.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

For years, Eli had let his older cousin Dax speak for him. When waiters asked Eli what he wanted, Dax answered. When teachers asked Eli a question, Dax leaned in and whispered the reply. Eli told himself he was just shy. But on the bus to the championship, when the coach asked who would take the final shot, Eli felt the old silence rising in his throat, and Dax already opening his mouth. This time Eli spoke first. 'I will,' he said, surprising even himself. Dax blinked and sat back. The words had been small, but the room they made inside Eli was enormous.

Which quotation best supports the inference that this moment marks a turning point in Eli's confidence? Quote it and explain how it shows change rather than just a single action.
items.answer: The best quotation is 'The words had been small, but the room they made inside Eli was enormous.' It supports the inference of a turning point because it shows the tiny act of speaking up created a huge internal change in Eli, signaling growth in his confidence rather than just one ordinary action.

steps: The inference is that this moment is a turning point in Eli's confidence, meaning a lasting change, not just one event.
'This time Eli spoke first' shows the action but not its larger meaning.
'The words had been small, but the room they made inside Eli was enormous' contrasts the small action with a huge inner effect, signaling real internal change.
Because it points to a large, lasting shift inside Eli, it best supports the inference of a turning point in his confidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The museum guard, Mr. Okafor, had stood beside the same painting for twenty-two years. Tourists hurried past it to reach the famous works in the next room, but Mr. Okafor knew every brushstroke of the quiet little harbor scene, the way the gray light fell on the water, the single gull no one ever noticed. Some days he spoke to the painting under his breath, pointing out a child who had finally stopped to look. When the museum announced the harbor scene would be sold, Mr. Okafor said nothing in the meeting. That night he stayed long after closing, standing before the painting in the dark as though saying goodbye to an old friend.

A reader claims the text directly states that Mr. Okafor loves the painting. Is 'Mr. Okafor loves the painting' an explicit statement or an inference? Identify two details the inference rests on.
items.answer: It is an inference, not an explicit statement. The text never says Mr. Okafor loves the painting; the reader infers it from details such as that he 'knew every brushstroke' of the scene after twenty-two years and that he stayed late 'standing before the painting in the dark as though saying goodbye to an old friend.'

steps: Search the text for a direct statement of love; there is none.
The passage instead describes his actions and knowledge: he knows every brushstroke and the gull no one notices.
It also shows him saying goodbye 'as though saying goodbye to an old friend,' a comparison rather than a statement of feeling.
Because the feeling is built from these actions and the comparison, 'Mr. Okafor loves the painting' is an inference, not something stated directly.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The drought had lasted all summer, and the corn stood brown and brittle in the fields. Mr. Halvers walked the rows each morning, kicking up dust, his jaw tight. His daughter Ruth watched from the porch as the sky stayed cloudless day after day. One evening a thin gray smudge appeared on the horizon. Mr. Halvers stopped at the fence and watched it without a word. Ruth ran out to him. 'Is it rain?' she asked. He did not answer at first. When the first cool drops finally struck the dust, raising tiny puffs at their feet, he closed his eyes and let out a long breath he seemed to have been holding for weeks.

Claim: The rain brings Mr. Halvers deep relief. Quote the single best detail and explain how it supports this claim more strongly than the others.
items.answer: The best detail is 'he closed his eyes and let out a long breath he seemed to have been holding for weeks.' It supports the claim because letting out a long held breath shows tension finally releasing, which conveys deep relief better than details that only show worry or the rain itself.

steps: The claim is that the rain brings Mr. Halvers deep relief.
Earlier details like 'his jaw tight' show worry, not relief, and 'the first cool drops finally struck the dust' shows the rain but not his feeling.
'he closed his eyes and let out a long breath he seemed to have been holding for weeks' shows long-held tension leaving his body.
Because releasing a breath held for weeks directly pictures relief after worry, it is the strongest support for the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Two brothers inherited their father's clock shop. Marcus wanted to modernize, to sell sleek digital displays and clear the dusty shelves. Leo wanted to keep repairing the old wind-up clocks no one else could fix. They argued for a month. Then one rainy afternoon an elderly woman came in carrying a battered mantel clock, her hands trembling. 'It was my husband's,' she said. 'It stopped the day he died. I cannot bear the silence.' Leo took it gently and worked for an hour while Marcus watched. When the clock finally ticked again, the woman wept. Marcus quietly took down the digital display in the window and set the woman's clock there instead.

Which quotation best supports the inference that Marcus changes his mind about the value of the old clocks? Quote it and explain why a different true detail would be weaker evidence.
items.answer: The best quotation is 'Marcus quietly took down the digital display in the window and set the woman's clock there instead.' It supports the inference of a change of mind because Marcus replaces the modern display he favored with a repaired old clock, showing he now sees value in the old work. A detail like 'Marcus wanted to modernize' would be weaker because it shows only his original view, not the change.

steps: The inference is that Marcus changes his mind and comes to value the old clocks.
'Marcus wanted to modernize' shows his starting position, the opposite of a change.
'Marcus quietly took down the digital display in the window and set the woman's clock there instead' shows him reversing his earlier plan after seeing the repaired clock matter to the woman.
Because this action shows a shift from his original view, it is the strongest evidence of a change of mind, while his earlier opinion is weaker evidence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The substitute teacher wrote her name on the board and turned to face thirty pairs of bored eyes. Within minutes paper airplanes were sailing across the room. She did not raise her voice. Instead she sat on the edge of the desk and began to tell a story, quietly, about a city buried under the sea. One by one the planes stopped flying. Students leaned forward. A boy in the back, who had not opened a book all year, asked what happened next. By the time the bell rang, no one had noticed the hour pass, and three students lingered to ask if the city was real.

A student says the line 'paper airplanes were sailing across the room' proves the substitute teacher is a skilled storyteller. Explain why this evidence does not support that claim, and name a quotation that does.
items.answer: The line 'paper airplanes were sailing across the room' does not support the claim because it describes the students misbehaving before she tells her story, showing the class out of control, not her skill. A quotation that does support the claim is 'One by one the planes stopped flying' (or that the boy 'who had not opened a book all year asked what happened next'), since it shows her story winning over even the most disengaged students.

steps: The claim is that the substitute is a skilled storyteller.
'paper airplanes were sailing across the room' describes the class misbehaving before she begins, so it shows disorder, not her storytelling skill.
Look later for the effect of her story: 'One by one the planes stopped flying' and the unmotivated boy asking 'what happened next' show her story capturing the class.
These later details support the claim because they show even disengaged students drawn in, while the airplane line is off the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The poem reads:

The old oak does not beg the storm for mercy.
It bends its great arms low and lets them shake,
releasing one by one its yellowed leaves
to save the deeper branches it would keep.
When morning comes the field is gold with loss,
yet rooted still, the oak stands taller, bare,
and greets the cold blue light without complaint,
as if some lesser self had blown away.

Claim: The poem suggests that giving something up can be a kind of strength. Quote one line and explain how its figurative meaning supports this claim.
items.answer: A supporting line is 'releasing one by one its yellowed leaves to save the deeper branches it would keep.' Figuratively, the oak gives up its leaves on purpose to protect what matters most, which shows that letting go can be a wise, strong choice rather than a weakness, supporting the claim. (The closing line 'as if some lesser self had blown away' also works.)

steps: The claim is that giving something up can be a kind of strength.
Read the figurative action: the oak releases its leaves on purpose 'to save the deeper branches it would keep.'
This shows a deliberate sacrifice that protects what is most important, framing loss as a wise choice.
Paired with 'the oak stands taller, bare,' the giving up leads to strength, so the line supports the claim that letting go can be strength.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Every Saturday, Nadia volunteered at the animal shelter, but she always avoided the back kennel where the old three-legged dog named Biscuit waited. He never barked. He just pressed his nose to the wire and watched her pass. Nadia told the staff she was too busy to walk him, that the younger dogs needed her more. One rainy Saturday the shelter was nearly empty, and she had no excuse. She clipped a leash on Biscuit and walked him slowly around the block. He limped along beside her, leaning into her leg at every corner. When they returned, she sat down on the wet pavement and let him put his graying head in her lap, and she did not get up for a long time.

A reader offers three quotations to prove the inference 'Nadia had been avoiding Biscuit because his quiet need made her uncomfortable, until she finally let herself care for him.' Quote the single strongest line for this inference and explain why the others are weaker.
items.answer: The strongest line is 'she sat down on the wet pavement and let him put his graying head in her lap, and she did not get up for a long time.' It shows Nadia finally letting herself care for Biscuit and forming a bond, which captures the heart of the inference. Lines like 'she always avoided the back kennel' show only the avoidance, and 'she was too busy' is an excuse, so each shows just one part rather than the full change the inference describes.

steps: The inference has two parts: Nadia avoided Biscuit because his quiet need was uncomfortable, and she finally lets herself care for him.
'she always avoided the back kennel' shows only the avoidance, and 'too busy' is just the excuse, so each covers one part.
'she sat down on the wet pavement and let him put his graying head in her lap, and she did not get up for a long time' shows her finally accepting the connection she had been avoiding.
Because it captures the resolution of the avoidance into care, it is the strongest evidence for the full inference.
